1387.title: The ten-day retreat, the hard days
1387.hook: some days of the retreat are hard; the practice is to stay
1387.howItsDone: On ten-day retreats, students are encouraged to stay through the difficult days, and some courses include sittings in which students try not to move, observing discomfort and restlessness as they arise and pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the retreat began: the phone in an envelope, noble silence, a bell before dawn, the breath at the nostrils. Your line was day one.

Somewhere in the middle of a ten-day retreat, a sensible plan forms in the mind. The car is in the lot. The keys are in the bag. Nobody would really mind. The knees ache, the back aches, the breath is boring, and every old song and old argument is playing at once. People who have sat these retreats tell stories about this moment; some can name the very day it came. Not everyone hits it on the same day, and some never hit it at all.
screen: `THE CAR IS IN THE LOT.` → `THE KNEES, THE BACK, THE SONGS.` → `THE HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, why it gets hard. On day one, the newness carries you. A day or so later it's gone, and what's left is you, the cushion, and everything you'd usually drown out with a phone. Further in, as the practice deepens, old feelings can rise to the surface. Teachers on these courses say this is expected, not a sign that something has gone wrong. Second, the instruction: stay. Some retreats include sittings where students try not to move at all, not shifting the legs or opening the eyes, simply watching what comes up. An ache rises, peaks, changes, fades. Restlessness rises and fades. Underneath is impermanence: nothing that arises stays. Third, an old story about staying the right way. In the Numerical Discourses, a monk named Sona practices so hard, pacing in walking meditation, that his feet bleed, and he thinks of giving up and going home. The Buddha asks him: when you played the lute, did it sound right with the strings too tight? No. Too loose? No. Only when tuned just right. Effort, the Buddha says, is like that: neither strained nor slack. Sona stays, and in the story he goes on to awakening. Fourth, what staying means. Not gritting your teeth until you break; not running, and not forcing. Sit with the ache. Breathe. Adjust the string if you need to. Then stay a little longer than the plan in your head said you could.
screen: `THE NEWNESS WEARS OFF.` · `AN ACHE RISES, AND FADES.` · `SONA'S LUTE: NOT TOO TIGHT.` · `STAYING ISN'T STRAINING.` · then, large: `STAY.`

segments.voice: Settle in and breathe, and when something wants your attention, an itch, a stiff shoulder, the urge to check the time, stay with it a few breaths and notice where it is and whether it changes. If it's real or sharp pain, move gently; that's tuning the string, not failing. If it's only restlessness, see whether you can stay one breath longer than you wanted.
The ten-day retreat. On the hard days, the practice is simply to stay, with effort tuned like a lute string, neither too tight nor too loose. Today's word.
Your line: stay. Not too tight, not too loose. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1387 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TEN-DAY RETREAT, METTA DAY.`

1388.title: The ten-day retreat, metta day
1388.hook: the last day's metta and the return to talking
1388.howItsDone: At the end of ten-day retreats in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, students practice metta, loving-kindness toward all beings, before noble silence is lifted and they begin talking with one another again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hard days, and Sona's lute: effort neither too tight nor too loose. Your line was stay. Metta first came up on day 15, a wish for people you don't like; today it closes the retreat.

For days, the dining hall has sounded like spoons and footsteps. Then, near the end of the retreat, silence lifts, and the first words come out as whispers, as if talking were a language half forgotten. Someone laughs. Then the room roars. People who passed each other again and again without a glance find out names, hometowns, what nearly made them leave. But before anyone says a word, there's one more sit, and it's different from all the others.
screen: `SPOONS AND FOOTSTEPS.` → `THE FIRST WHISPERS.` → `THE ROOM ROARS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Metta is the Pali word for loving-kindness, or friendliness: a warm wish for the well-being of others, with no strings attached. Second, why it comes last. In courses taught in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, the long days of watching breath and body are followed by a session of metta before silence lifts. As those teachers give it, a mind made calmer and clearer by days of practice has something to share, and metta is the sharing. You've done the work; now give away what it earned. Third, the old text. In the discourse on loving-kindness, a short teaching in the collection called the Sutta Nipata, the Buddha describes the heart to cultivate. As a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so one should keep a boundless heart toward all beings: above, below, all around, without hatred or ill will. Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as one is awake, the text says, keep this mindfulness. Fourth, the return to talking. Metta isn't left on the cushion. The first test comes minutes later, in a noisy room, with the person who sniffled through every sit, or the one who took your spot. The practice changes shape: from watching your own mind to wishing others well, out loud and face to face. Some students say the talking feels harder than the silence was.
screen: `METTA: LOVING-KINDNESS.` · `THE LAST SIT GIVES IT AWAY.` · `LIKE A MOTHER WITH HER ONLY CHILD.` · `THE FIRST TEST IS THE DINING HALL.` · then, large: `TOWARD ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Begin with the breath, letting the mind quiet, then bring to mind someone you love and wish them well with the simple words teachers often give: may you be well, may you be safe, may you be at ease. Widen it to someone you barely know, then someone difficult, then everyone, in every direction. If the warmth won't come, that's all right; the wish still counts.
The ten-day retreat. At its end, a sit of metta, loving-kindness toward all beings, and then silence lifts and the talking begins. Today's word.
Your line: metta day. The silence ends, and the wishing goes on. Until tomorrow.

1389.title: The ten-day retreat, going home
1389.hook: the hardest part: carrying the calm into ordinary life
1389.howItsDone: After a meditation retreat, Buddhist teachers commonly encourage students to keep a regular practice at home, such as a daily sit, and to bring the retreat's attention into work, family and ordinary errands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, metta day: a last sit of loving-kindness, then silence lifts and the dining hall roars. Your line was metta day.

The envelope comes back. Inside, the phone, and when it wakes it starts buzzing and doesn't stop: messages, alerts, a calendar full of next week. The drive home has traffic. The grocery store on the way is louder than you remember, and brighter. Someone cuts in line, and something old and hot rises in the chest, right on schedule. On the last morning, the calm felt solid enough to stand on. By dinner, it's thinner. Teachers of these retreats often say this is where the real work starts.
screen: `THE PHONE STARTS BUZZING.` → `SOMEONE CUTS IN LINE.` → `THE CALM GROWS THIN.`

segments.voice: First, the thinning. A retreat's calm was made in special conditions: silence, bells, no choices. Out here those conditions are gone, and the calm fades. Teachers say that's normal, and that the calm was never really the point. The point was learning to see the mind, and that can come home. Second, an old Zen picture of it. The ox-herding pictures are a series of Zen images. A herder searches for a lost ox, a picture of the mind, finds its tracks, catches it, tames it, rides it home. Then herder and ox both vanish into an empty circle. But the series doesn't stop there. In its last picture, the herder walks into the town marketplace, barefoot, belly round, hands open, mixing with ordinary people. The verse with it says he has no need of special powers; the withered trees bloom wherever he goes. The path doesn't end on the mountain. It ends in the market. Third, one habit. Teachers on retreat courses encourage some practice at home: a sit in the morning or evening, a pause before eating, a day of silence now and then. Some students go home vowing to keep everything and keep nothing. One habit, kept, carries further. Fourth, the test. The person who cuts in line, the coworker, the family at the dinner table: that's where the practice now lives. The retreat wasn't an escape from ordinary life. It was training for it.
screen: `THE CALM GROWS THIN.` · `THE OX-HERDER REACHES THE MARKET.` · `ONE HABIT, KEPT.` · `THE PRACTICE LIVES AT HOME NOW.` · then, large: `HANDS OPEN, IN THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe, then choose one retreat habit small enough to do even on a bad day: a few breaths before you look at your phone, a pause before meals, a short sit at night. See yourself doing it tomorrow, in your actual kitchen, then let the choice rest and come back to the breath.
The ten-day retreat. Its last lesson comes after it ends: carrying what was learned in silence back into traffic, kitchens and crowded rooms. Today's word.
Your line: carry it home. The retreat ends the moment you drive away, and then, slowly, it begins again. Same time tomorrow.

1390.title: Sesshin, the first days
1390.hook: the sore legs, the bells, the long hours
1390.howItsDone: Zen Buddhists in Japan and at Zen centers elsewhere hold sesshin, retreats of several days in silence, alternating seated zazen with walking kinhin, eating formal meals in the meditation hall, and meeting privately with the teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the retreat ended, and the ox-herder walked into the marketplace with open hands. Your line was carry it home.

Nobody warns you properly about the knees. In a Zen hall, a row of people sits facing the wall on black cushions, legs folded. A bell rings to begin. For a while, everything is fine. Then a dull ache starts in the left knee. Then the right ankle. Then a buzzing in the foot that slowly turns into no feeling at all. The wall doesn't change. The bell hasn't rung yet. Somewhere behind you, slow footsteps pass along the row.
screen: `FACING THE WALL.` → `THE LEFT KNEE, THE RIGHT ANKLE.` → `THE BELL HASN'T RUNG.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Sesshin is the Japanese Zen name for an intensive retreat of several days; teachers often explain it as gathering the mind, or touching the mind. Second, the day. It's built of periods of zazen, seated meditation, with slow walking meditation, called kinhin, in between, so the legs can move. Wooden sounds and bells mark every change: a struck board calls people to the hall, a bell starts and ends the sitting, clappers signal meals. Meals are often eaten in the hall in silence, with a formal set of bowls. There are talks by the teacher, and private meetings where a student can bring a question. Most of the day, though, is sitting. Third, the legs. Zen posture comes from old instructions like those of the Japanese teacher Dogen, who advised full or half lotus, back upright, not leaning to either side, forward or back. In the first days, the body protests. Teachers say the ache is not the enemy. It's information, a chance to see how the mind reacts: the stories it tells, the bargains it makes, the clock it keeps checking. Some Zen centers now offer benches and chairs, and teachers distinguish ordinary ache from the kind of pain that means move. Fourth, those footsteps. In some halls, a monitor carries a flat wooden stick, the keisaku. A drowsy or tense sitter may ask for it with a bow, and receives a few sharp taps on the shoulders. It isn't punishment. It's offered as help, and received with a bow.
screen: `GATHERING THE MIND.` · `SIT, WALK, SIT AGAIN.` · `THE ACHE IS INFORMATION.` · `THE STICK IS HELP, ASKED FOR.` · then, large: `SORE LEGS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright in whatever position you'll stay in, a chair, a cushion, the edge of a bed, and when some small discomfort comes, listen less to the body and more to the mind's commentary. Give each piece a quiet name, story, bargain, clock, then return to the plain sensation underneath. If it's sharp pain, move.
Sesshin. A Zen retreat of several days, of sitting and walking meditation, bells and silence, and, in the first days, sore legs. Today's word.
Your line: sore legs. The legs speak first, and the mind answers. Rest well.

1391.title: Sesshin, the last day
1391.hook: stillness, and the tea at the end
1391.howItsDone: Zen sesshin end in different ways from hall to hall; in some, tea is served to each sitter in silence before the retreat closes and talking resumes, and tea itself is prepared and drunk as a practice of attention in Zen communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first days of sesshin: the wall, the bells, the stick asked for with a bow. Your line was sore legs. You first met Zhaozhou's tea on day 988; today, it ends a retreat.

By the last morning of sesshin, the hall sounds different. The same bells, the same wall, the same rows of cushions. But the shuffling has stopped. Nobody shifts their weight every few minutes. The ache in the knee may still be there, but the arguing about it has gone quiet. Then the final bell rings, and it doesn't call anyone to sit again. Someone comes down the row with a kettle. A small cup is set before each person, and tea is poured.
screen: `THE SHUFFLING STOPS.` → `THE FINAL BELL.` → `A KETTLE COMES DOWN THE ROW.`

segments.voice: First, the stillness. Some students who sit sesshin describe the later days as quieter, not because the mind has gone blank, but because it has stopped fighting the schedule. The bells ring and the body goes. Sitting has become ordinary, and some Zen teachers say that ordinariness is closer to the point than any fireworks. Second, tea in Zen. Tea and Zen have kept company for a long time in China and Japan. Tradition says monks drank it to stay awake through long sittings, and serving tea became a practice of its own, done with full attention. Some sesshins end with tea served in the hall, simply, in silence, before talking begins. Third, an old Zen story. The Chinese teacher Zhaozhou asks a newly arrived monk, have you been here before? Yes, says the monk. Go have some tea. He asks another. No, says the second monk. Go have some tea. The puzzled temple steward asks why he told both the same thing. Zhaozhou calls his name. The steward answers. Go have some tea. Whatever you've done or not done, whatever you know or don't, the next thing is the cup in front of you. Fourth, the tea at the end. After days of effort, the last teaching is a warm cup held in two hands, drunk slowly, with nothing to achieve. No insight announced. Just tea, and then people get up, wash the cups, and go home.
screen: `STILLNESS IS ORDINARY.` · `TEA, DRUNK WITH FULL ATTENTION.` · `ZHAOZHOU: GO HAVE SOME TEA.` · `NOTHING LEFT TO ACHIEVE.` · then, large: `THE TEA AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Hold a cup of tea, coffee or water in both hands, or hold your empty hands as if a cup were in them, and feel its warmth or coolness and its weight. Bring it to your lips slowly and take one small sip, tasting it fully, then set it down and breathe. Nothing to figure out, nothing to finish: just this cup, and then this one.
Sesshin. A Zen retreat of several days, which, in some halls, ends not with a speech but with stillness, and a small cup of tea. Today's word.
Your line: the tea at the end. Been here before or not: tea. See you tomorrow.

1392.title: Pilgrimage: Lumbini
1392.hook: the garden of the birth in Nepal, with Ashoka's pillar
1392.howItsDone: Buddhists from many countries and schools travel to Lumbini in Nepal, where they walk the sacred garden, see Ashoka's pillar and the site honored as the Buddha's birthplace, and sit, chant or meditate there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day of sesshin: long silence, then a cup of tea. Your line was the tea at the end. You first met Lumbini on day 23; now the path goes there on pilgrimage.

Near the border of Nepal and India is a garden with a pond, old brick foundations, and trees hung with bright prayer flags that snap in the wind. Monks walk the brick paths slowly; a family spreads a cloth on the grass by the water. In the middle stands a plain stone pillar, weathered and gray, with lines of very old writing cut into it. People come from far away to stand next to that pillar for a minute. Then some sit under a tree and say nothing at all. The place is Lumbini, where the story starts.
screen: `A GARDEN NEAR THE BORDER.` → `A PLAIN STONE PILLAR.` → `WHERE THE STORY STARTS.`

segments.voice: Start with the oldest reason for going. In the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, the Buddha, near the end of his life, tells his attendant Ananda that there are places a person of faith may visit and be moved. The first is where you can say: here the Tathagata was born. Tathagata is a name the Buddha uses for himself in the texts. So pilgrimage isn't something later Buddhists invented on their own; in the text, the Buddha points to it himself. Now the garden. In the Sutta Nipata, an old collection of verses, gods announce the birth of a future Buddha in the Lumbini country, among the Sakyas. Later tellings fill in the scene: Queen Maya on her way to her family's home, stopping in a garden, reaching up to a branch of a tree, and giving birth standing. Tradition tells that part with great tenderness. Then the pillar. The emperor Ashoka, who turned toward the Buddha's teaching after a bloody war, set up stone pillars across his lands. The one at Lumbini, as scholars read its inscription, records that he came here himself and honored the place because the Buddha was born here. A king walking into a garden to stand where a baby was born: that's the whole shape of pilgrimage. Nothing happens at Lumbini that couldn't happen at home. You walk, you arrive, you stand, and you remember. The place doesn't teach. It helps you remember the one who did.
screen: `THE BUDDHA NAMES THE PLACES.` · `QUEEN MAYA AND THE TREE.` · `A KING CAME TO THIS GARDEN.` · then, large: `HERE HE WAS BORN.`

segments.voice: Close or lower your eyes and picture the garden: grass, a still pond, prayer flags moving, the gray pillar in the sun. Sit under a tree in your mind and let the thought settle: a child was born here, and that child became a teacher. If your mind wanders to your own day, walk back into the garden.
Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, made to remember. In the Buddha's own words, the first of the places worth seeing is where he was born. Today's word.
Your line: where he was born. A garden, a pillar, a long road. Until tomorrow.

1393.title: Pilgrimage: Bodh Gaya
1393.hook: the Mahabodhi temple and the bodhi tree, full of pilgrims from every school
1393.howItsDone: Pilgrims from many Buddhist schools come to Bodh Gaya in India to circle the Mahabodhi temple, sit or prostrate near the bodhi tree, chant, and offer flowers, lamps and robes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lumbini: a garden and a king's stone pillar. Your line was where he was born. Day 51 told the night under the tree; today, the place itself.

Before sunrise, the sound starts. A Tibetan monk on a cushion on the flagstones reads aloud from a long, loose-leaf text. A few steps away, a group in white chants in Pali. Further on, Japanese pilgrims in a line strike a small hand drum. A woman from Thailand presses gold leaf onto a railing. Above them rises a tall carved tower, and behind it a broad tree with heart-shaped leaves, its branches propped up and draped in cloth. They don't all practice alike. They have all walked to the same tree. This is Bodh Gaya, and they remember it in plain words: here he woke up.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, MANY SCHOOLS.` → `A TOWER AND A TREE.` → `HERE HE WOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Start with why he went there. In the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha looks back on his search. He had studied with teachers and left them, still unsatisfied. Then he walked until he reached Uruvela, and found what he calls a delightful grove, with a clear river and a village nearby for alms: a good place, he says, for someone set on striving. So he sat down. He didn't pick a holy place. He picked a good place, and it became holy because of what happened there. Next, the tree. Bodhi means awakening; the tree is named for the night, not the other way around. The opening of the monastic rule picks up just after: the Buddha sitting at the foot of the bodhi tree by the river, newly awakened, staying on in the joy of freedom. Today's tree isn't the same trunk. Tradition says it comes down from the first through cuttings carried and replanted, and pilgrims treat it with that care. Then the temple. The Mahabodhi temple rises beside the tree, and near it a stone seat marks where tradition says he sat. And here's what a visitor carries home. At Bodh Gaya, Theravada, Tibetan, Zen, Pure Land and newer communities have built monasteries and practice side by side. This path has met the schools one at a time, chant by chant. At the tree, they share one shade.
screen: `A DELIGHTFUL GROVE BY A RIVER.` · `BODHI MEANS AWAKENING.` · `ONE TREE, MANY SCHOOLS.` · then, large: `HERE HE WOKE.`

segments.voice: Sit with your back straight and easy, and picture the tree: wide branches, leaves trembling, many chants at once. Sit beneath it in your mind; you don't need to wake up today, just sit where someone once did, and breathe. When your thoughts wander, come back to the leaves.
Pilgrimage. A journey to remember. Its second great stop is Bodh Gaya, where the tree and the temple mark the Buddha's awakening. Today's word.
Your line: where he woke. Not a holy place to begin with, just a good one. Rest well.

chat.says: Why is one tree in India so important to Buddhists from every country?
options: The Buddha woke under the bodhi tree there, and now many schools share its shade.
It's a tree the Buddha planted himself, and its leaves are said to heal the sick.
It's where the Buddha was born, so every school begins its calendar there.
chat.meaning: Bodh Gaya is where the Buddha awakened at the foot of the bodhi tree. Theravada, Tibetan, Zen, Pure Land and newer communities now practice there side by side.
